glaciolacustrine: Laid down on the bed of a lake fed by melting glaciers. Glaciolacustrine soils are often fine silts and clays in thin layers, and can be much weaker than the glacial till around them.
strain-softening: Losing strength as a soil keeps deforming after it has reached its peak strength; also called strain weakening. A slip on a strain-softening soil can speed up once it starts, because the ground grips less the further it moves.
peak-strength: The greatest shear stress a soil can carry, reached after a small movement. A strain-softening soil then falls toward a lower strength as it keeps moving.
site-investigation: Finding out what the ground under a planned structure is made of, layer by layer, and how strong and permeable each layer is: by mapping the geology, drilling boreholes, testing in the holes and testing samples in a laboratory.
borehole: A narrow hole drilled into the ground to see, test and sample what lies below. A borehole tells you only about the ground it passes through.
